A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same image-geolocation privacy study, substantially expanded in v3. Their text, figures, tables, equations and appendices support comparison, including v1's screenshot-based appendix.

before.justification: v1 reports original o3 geolocation results on 50 images, visual-clue frequencies and paired masking demonstrations.

after.justification: v3 reports original model evaluations on DOXBENCH, reasoning and tool-use analyses, GEOMINER experiments, human comparisons and defense results.

M1.justification: v1 queries o3 and manually categorizes its clues. v3 introduces CLUEMINER's iterative analyzer and category-memory procedure, plus GEOMINER's two-stage Detector–Analyzer inference pipeline (Sections 5.3 and 6; Appendix B). These are new procedural components, beyond renaming the earlier clue analysis.

E1.justification: The benchmark changes from Google Maps residential imagery across US cities to researcher-captured California imagery spanning three privacy-risk levels. New coverage includes private spaces without individuals, 46 reflection cases and explicit benign defense controls. Public travel scenes themselves are not wholly new: v1 already includes such appendix demonstrations.

E2.justification: v1 evaluates o3 without model or human comparators. v3 adds comparisons involving o4-mini, GPT-4o, GPT-4.1, Gemini 2.5 Pro, Claude 4, QVQ-Max and Llama 4 models. GEOMINER is compared with vanilla and CoT prompting, and Table 4 introduces non-expert human performance.

E3.justification: v1 Figure 3 selects the most accurate prediction across four prompts; v3 separately evaluates structured Top-1/Top-3 and vanilla/CoT conditions. Distance bins and one-/five-mile labels give way to geodesic AED/MED, Census-based geographic accuracy, VRR and GLARE. v3 also introduces API-versus-web/tool controls and a 30-image human comparison with a 300-second limit.

E4.justification: v1's paired Suzhou and Cleveland masking demonstrations are removed. v3 adds reasoning-pattern audits, CoT and tool-use comparisons, CLUEMINER convergence analysis, reflection case studies, Gaussian-noise sensitivity, and prompt/guardrail defense tests. These substantially broaden the mechanisms and failure conditions investigated.

E5.justification: v3 newly reports IQR-based outlier filtering for Table 1, changing the documented statistical treatment of errors. Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals or significance tests.

E6.justification: v1's headline results are 60% within one mile and 84% within five miles. Under its different dataset and protocol, v3 Table 1 reports o3 vanilla Top-1 VRR of 80.8%, AED of 13.56 km and 34 correct census-block predictions; these are not comparable performance changes. Extensive new results cover other models, reflections, GEOMINER, humans and defenses.

T1.justification: v1's autoregressive factorization and image-set formalization are removed. v3 introduces GLARE's mutual-information definition, entropy bound, uniform spatial assumptions, spherical-cap approximation and geometric-mean error radius (Appendix C). This is substantial new mathematical content, although the derivation unjustifiably replaces the bound I(L;R) ≤ H(R) with equality.

C1.justification: The o3-specific accuracy and masking contributions become a broader cross-model privacy-risk claim. v3 foregrounds DOXBENCH, three risk levels, CLUEMINER, GEOMINER and GLARE, claims advantages over non-expert humans, and identifies clue-based reasoning and insufficient privacy alignment as two principal causes.

C2.justification: v1 emphasizes revealing clues and the potential of targeted masking, qualified by residual-clue leakage. v3 adds interpretations of CoT answering harder previously refused cases, tool amplification and reflection-related exposure. Its defense discussion develops noise-dependent failures and privacy–utility tradeoffs from prompt-based refusal, substantially expanding applicability and limitation analysis.

D1.justification: v3 documents camera/EXIF data collection, framework and defense prompts, default model parameters, geocoding/Census/pyproj evaluation, and noise-processing libraries and settings. It adds a project URL and removes v1's explicit dataset non-release statement. The PDFs alone do not establish that code or data actually became downloadable.

R1.justification: v3 adds engagement with VLMs as GeoGuessr Masters and Image-based Geolocation Using Large Vision-Language Models, criticizing image resolution, privacy coverage and evaluation practices. Positioning expands around a risk-tiered benchmark, legal/privacy-policy context and information-theoretic measurement, while retaining the earlier distinction between inference-time and training-data privacy.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion are extensively rewritten around three research questions. The earlier compact methodology/experiment narrative becomes separate threat-model, evaluation, mechanism, attack, human-comparison and defense sections. The screenshot appendix is replaced by organized Appendices A–D covering ethics, methods, mathematics and prompts.

P2.justification: The opening illustrative example is retained, but most displays are redesigned or replaced. v1's collection workflow, clue-frequency plots and full-page appendix chats give way to risk-level examples and radar charts, multi-model tables, convergence/attack/noise plots and prompt boxes. This substantially changes visual organization beyond numerical updates.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens the empirical foundation beyond v1's single-model pilot through model/human comparators, refusal reporting, Census-based accuracy and controlled mechanism/defense tests. These address important weaknesses in interpreting the original leakage claims. The new GLARE contribution remains materially flawed: Appendix C substitutes an entropy bound with equality, and Table 4's bit values are roughly 100 times those implied by its formula. This weakens information-theoretic claims, but the independent conventional metrics and comparisons still provide substantial overall gains.
